claim.text: Iterative magnitude pruning with layerwise magnitude selection in a binary sentiment analysis task on five Amazon Reviews domains (Books, Electronics, Movies, CDs, Home) using a CNN with three filter heights $h\in\{3,4,5\}$, each with 127 channels, ReLU activation, 1-max pooling, one hidden MLP layer of dimension 117, embedding dimension $d=417$, max sequence length $n=500$, embeddings initialized from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and convolutional/MLP layers initialized with He initialization, trained with Adam at learning rate $1\mathrm{e}{-3}$, $\ell_2$ weight $1\mathrm{e}{-5}$, batch size 32, dropout $p=0.285$, produces sparse subnetworks (tickets) that, when reinitialized to their original initial values (TICKET-RESET) and retrained in isolation, achieve test accuracy comparable to or better than the unpruned full model (FULL-MODEL) for moderate sparsity levels, with TICKET-RESET outperforming FULL-MODEL in the early-to-moderate sparsification regime (approximately 0%–90% sparsity) for the Books, Electronics, and Home domains.

In the setting of note 1, resetting the retained weights of a sparse subnetwork to random draws from the original initialization distributions (TICKET-RANDOM) yields test performance statistically similar to resetting to the original initial values (TICKET-RESET) for sparsity levels up to approximately 96%.

Using the five Amazon Reviews domains (Books, Electronics, Movies, CDs, Home) and the CNN architecture (three filter heights $h\in\{3,4,5\}$, 127 channels, ReLU, 1-max pooling, MLP dim 117, embedding dim 417, max seq length 500, embeddings from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, conv/MLP He initialization (weights from $\mathcal{U}(-b,b)$ with $b=\sqrt{6/((1+a^2)\times\text{fan\_in})}$), Adam lr $1\mathrm{e}{-3}$, $\ell_2$ weight $1\mathrm{e}{-5}$, batch size 32, dropout $p=0.285$) with iterative magnitude pruning ($p=35\%$, $r_{total}=20$), a phase transition occurs at approximately $96\%$ sparsity: beyond this threshold, subnetworks reinitialized to random draws from the original initialization distributions (TICKET-RANDOM) exhibit rapid test accuracy degradation and high instability, whereas subnetworks reinitialized to their original initial values (TICKET-RESET) maintain substantially better and more stable test accuracy, even at sparsity levels exceeding $99.9\%$.

The choice of initialization—whether subnetworks are reinitialized to random draws from the original initialization distributions (TICKET-RANDOM) or to their original initial values (TICKET-RESET)—is largely immaterial below approximately 96% sparsity but becomes crucial for preserving accuracy and reducing variance in the extreme-sparsity regime.

Under the iterative magnitude pruning procedure (prune fraction $p=35\%$, $r_{total}=20$) with the CNN architecture and training details (five Amazon Reviews domains, CNN with filters $h\in\{3,4,5\}$, 127 channels, ReLU, 1-max pooling, MLP dim 117, embedding dim 417, max seq length 500, embeddings from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, conv/MLP He initialization (weights from $\mathcal{U}(-b,b)$ with $b=\sqrt{6/((1+a^2)\times\text{fan\_in})}$), Adam lr $1\mathrm{e}{-3}$, $\ell_2$ weight $1\mathrm{e}{-5}$, batch size 32, dropout $p=0.285$), when sparse masks $m$ obtained from a source domain $\mathcal{D}_s$ are applied to a target domain $\mathcal{D}_t$ (with $\mathcal{D}_s \neq \mathcal{D}_t$) and the retained parameters are reinitialized either to the source-domain original values (MASKS-RESET) or to random draws from the original initialization distributions (MASKS-RANDOM), the resulting subnetworks retrain in the target domain with only modest accuracy degradation relative to tickets obtained directly in the target domain via the same procedure (TICKET-TARGET) for sparsity levels up to approximately $90\%$.

Across the five Amazon review domains (Books, Electronics, Movies, CDs, Home) under the lottery ticket transfer procedure masks obtained from the CDs domain and applied to any other target domain outperform the subnetworks obtained directly in that target domain and retain stronger performance even at sparsity levels exceeding $99\%$.
